docs.title: 12. Attribution boundary
docs.text:
Giving full credit means being exact about who contributed what.

From Yuan & Recker (2015):

  • the three-aspect framework (content, development process, application context) and the user-support analysis;
  • the inventory of 14 rubrics and every count, percentage, and indicator name attributed to them above;
  • the use of validity, reliability, and utility as the criteria for judging a rubric (the definitions themselves are cited by the authors to Kimberlin & Winterstein, 2008, and Moskal & Leydens, 2000), and the conclusion that scales, scoring guides, testing, revision, and user support matter.

From the rubrics the review catalogued: the indicator names in the lineage columns belong to their original authors, listed in Section 13.

From this book's author:

  • the decision that reuse is a co-primary component of scoring (D1), and the principle that reuse applies to any content that can be easily reused in another textbook;
  • the "What is the Scientific Method" MicroSim and its quiz as the motivating example, from which the portability, reach, and substance factors are drawn;
  • the choice of the 0–3 scale with N/A (D2);
  • the decision to record social-authority signals and not score them (D3);
  • the acceptance of the agreement pass lines for V1, V2, and V5 (D4);
  • the decision to read every unit and sample nothing, and to run reuse judgments on all components (D5);
  • the principle "you can't reuse what you can't find", which sets the order of the reuse scoring process and the weight on findability (D11);
  • the approval of the anchor pattern (D6);
  • the requirement to differentiate a static image, which gives no feedback on student activity, from a fully interactive infographic that lets the textbook track viewing and estimate concept understanding from that activity (Section 4);
  • the decision that the headline is two numbers, one for overall quality and one for reusable content (D7);
  • the decision that a component with low content quality is never reuse-ready (D8);
  • the nine component types, including the FAQ question-answer pair (D9);
  • the packaging conventions for MicroSims, FAQs, quizzes, and static posters, as documented in the author's microsim-generator, faq-generator, and quiz-generator skills (Section 4);
  • the approval of the rules that make the pass lines operational (D10);
  • the decision to weight chapters by their number of concepts when rolling chapter scores up to the book (D12);
  • the observation that concepts are not equally weighted, and the decision to assume a roughly equal Concept Impact Score in the first release and defer a CIS-weighted roll-up (D12). The CIS measure itself is defined in this book's CONTENT-GENERATION-GUIDE.md;
  • the decision to count instrumentation once, beside the reuse value and not within it (D13);
  • the approval of how Q and R are computed (D14);
  • the approval of the findability mechanism: the stage-1 cutoff, the reuse value formula, and the retrieval test (D11);
  • the search tool and its calibration, from the author's search-microsims project: the reuse mode, the catalog, the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 WHAT vectors, the reuse (0.75) and template (0.60) bands, the duplicate clusters, and the metadata-quality metrics that motivated the RP5 split (Section 6);
  • the decisions on the improvement list: two skills, list only, prioritized by lowest effort and highest reward assuming an LLM tool, and deterministic items only in the first release (D15 to D18). The finding-to-skill mapping uses the author's existing skills and scripts.

Added by this book, not claimed by the review's authors:

  • the two-tier split into scripted checks and anchored LLM judgments;
  • the application to LLM and agent-skill evaluation, which the 2015 article does not address;
  • the component and bundle units, the reuse checks RP1–RP9, the reuse judgments RJ1–RJ7, the four-stage reuse process and its default formula, and validation steps V5 and V6. The review treats reuse as one indicator or one emphasis and does not decompose it;
  • the interactivity levels L0 to L2 and the learner-data indicators RP8, RP9, and RJ7. The review's interactivity indicators (Kurilovas et al.: "Interactivity level"; Achieve OER: "Quality of technological interactivity") rate how interactive a resource is, and none of the indicator names the review lists concerns recording learner activity;
  • the operational questions, the anchors, the ISE level, the output record, and the validation protocol;
  • the dimension groupings in Section 3.

Where this page reads the review's Appendix and draws a conclusion the text does not state (Section 2), it says so.

docs.title: Character Sheet: Echo the Loon
docs.text: The canonical identity document for Echo, the pedagogical mascot for the OER Evaluator textbook. Every pose prompt and every piece of AI-generated content involving this character must re-anchor to the description below. It is the source of truth for visual and voice consistency.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
• Name: Echo
  • Species: Loon
  • Subject: Evaluating and improving open educational resources (OER)
  • Catchphrase: "Let's dive in and check the evidence!"
  • Pronouns: Echo has no gender. Write "Echo" or they/them.

docs.title: Visual Description
docs.text:
• Body color: Glossy near-black head and neck with a white belly and a black back covered in a white checkered pattern, as on a common loon. Hex #1a1a2e for the black.
  • Accent color: Indigo, hex #3949ab, with a burnt-orange accent, hex #b45309. These match the book's indigo and orange theme.
  • Clothing / accessories: A small indigo scarf, and a magnifying glass with an orange handle held in one wing. Echo also has the loon's red eye.
  • Expression: Calm, sharp-eyed, and friendly, with a small closed-beak smile.
  • Size proportion: Small and compact, suitable for icon-sized display at about 90 pixels.
  • Art style: Flat cartoon illustration, modern vector, clean lines.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
• Patient: Echo never rushes a reviewer or a learner.
  • Sharp-eyed: Echo notices the detail others skip, such as a missing license or a broken link.
  • Encouraging: Echo treats mistakes as part of the process and celebrates progress.
  • Gently skeptical: Echo checks before trusting, especially an AI agent's confident answer.

docs.title: Voice
docs.text:
• Short, calm sentences that name the specific thing to check.
  • Asks "What is the evidence?" before accepting a claim, and models checking the work.
  • Uses water words sparingly and only when they fit: dive in, below the surface, ripples, calling across the lake. Never more than one per admonition.
  • Signature phrases: "Let's dive in and check the evidence!", "Look below the surface.", "Credit it, share it, pass it on."

docs.title: Why This Mascot
docs.text: A loon dives beneath the surface to see what is really there, which is what this book asks teachers to do when they check evidence and verify what an AI agent reports. A loon's call carries across a whole lake, which fits the idea of sharing and reusing OER, and the name Echo says the same thing. The loon is also Minnesota's state bird, which ties the book to the Minneapolis workshop it supports.

docs.title: Learning Graph for OER Evaluator
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement View the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 6 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
• Target Audience (4 of 5): four roles are named (K-12 teachers, college instructors, instructional designers, librarians and OER coordinators). The reading level and examples may need to favor one group. This slightly weakens the audience signal the learning graph uses to set concept depth.
  • Main Topics (9 of 10): the 18 topics are all relevant, but several overlap, such as the two metric topics and the two A/B testing topics. Overlap can produce duplicate concepts in the graph.

Two gaps are not scored by the rubric but matter for the book:

  • The 10 metrics have no scoring scale yet. The description names them and gives 10 points each, but does not say what earns a 10, a 5, or a 0. Chapters and the AI-agent prompts will need this.
  • The metrics are a proposal. They were drafted for the MNOP Pathfinder grant proposal, not taken from a published standard. The author should confirm or revise them.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
1. Define the scoring scale for each metric, with a short description of a 10, a 5, and a 0. This is the highest-value addition, because most chapters and sims depend on it.
  2. Merge overlapping topics if the learning graph comes out with duplicate concepts. For example, combine "Manual A/B testing" and "Analyzing A/B test results".
  3. Pick a primary audience for examples, for instance K-12 teachers, and note that the other roles can follow the same method.
  4. Cite external standards where the rubric borrows from them: the 5R permissions, WCAG 2.1 AA, Dublin Core, and Creative Commons licenses.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
Estimated concepts: about 220 to 280.

  • The 18 topics, at roughly 10 to 15 learnable concepts each, give about 180 to 270.
  • The 10 metrics each suggest several concepts of their own, such as the evidence a score needs, common failure cases, and fixes.
  • The Bloom's outcomes add process concepts, such as calibration, agreement, and error types.
  • This is an estimate. The learning-graph generator may find fewer after removing duplicates.

The description should support the 200-concept goal. If the generator falls short, the first place to add detail is the metric scoring scales.

docs.title: Sample One-Day Workshop Schedule
docs.text:
This workshop trains teachers to evaluate open educational resources (OER) for quality and reusability with AI agents, and then to use those agents to improve an OER they already teach with. Teachers arrive with one OER from their own subject and leave with an improved, openly licensed component and a checklist for earning the Certificate of OER Quality Evaluation Using AI Agents.

The day runs 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. and is designed for about 20 teachers. Every session uses the Sample Rubric Worksheet.

docs.title: Before the Workshop
docs.text:
Each teacher should:

  • Choose one OER they already use, such as a textbook chapter, a unit, a quiz, or an interactive simulation.
  • Bring a laptop with access to an AI agent tool.
  • Print or download the Sample Rubric Worksheet.

docs.title: Schedule
docs.text: Time Session What teachers leave with 8:30 to 9:00 Check-in and setup: log in to the AI tools and load the OER each teacher brought A working agent session 9:00 to 9:45 Why quality and reusability matter: the 10 metrics and how each is scored Rubric card 9:45 to 10:45 Calibration: pairs score a sample OER by hand, then run the agent and compare Hand and agent scores, with gaps explained 10:45 to 11:00 Break 11:00 to 12:00 Checking the agent: spot invented citations, misread licenses, and overconfident scores A verified evaluation of the sample 12:00 to 12:45 Lunch 12:45 to 2:15 Improvement challenge: use agents to raise one component's score by adding alt text, splitting content into reusable modules, writing metadata, generating practice questions, or building a simulation An improved component and its new score 2:15 to 2:30 Break 2:30 to 3:15 Peer review and publishing: swap and re-score each other's work, then publish under a CC BY license A published, openly licensed component 3:15 to 3:30 Next steps: certificate requirements and exit survey Certificate checklist

docs.title: After the Workshop
docs.text:
Teachers have 30 days to finish the certificate work described at the end of the Sample Rubric Worksheet. A reviewer checks each submission against the rubric before the certificate is issued.

The workshop sits inside a longer program, from building the rubric through the final report. See the Grant-Period Timeline.

docs.title: Sample Rubric Worksheet
docs.text:
This worksheet scores one open educational resource (OER) out of 100 points: 50 for quality and 50 for reusability, with 10 points per metric. Score each metric yourself, then record the AI agent's score beside yours so you can see where you and the agent disagree.

The reusability metrics follow the 5R permissions of open content: the right to retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute. These are sample metrics; they will be aligned with the chapters of this book as they are written.

Use it with the Sample One-Day Workshop Schedule.

docs.title: Resource Being Reviewed
docs.text: Field Entry Title URL License Subject and grade level Component reviewed (chapter, unit, quiz, or simulation) Reviewer Date

docs.title: Part 1: Quality (50 points)
docs.text: Metric What to check Your score (0 to 10) Agent score (0 to 10) Evidence Accuracy and currency Facts match cited sources; sources and data are current Alignment Each section maps to a stated learning outcome; Bloom's levels range from remember to create Readability Reading level fits the audience; terms are defined before use Accessibility Alt text, heading structure, captions, and color contrast (WCAG 2.1 AA) Practice with feedback Quizzes, worked examples, or interactive simulations that give feedback

docs.title: Part 2: Reusability (50 points)
docs.text: Metric What to check Your score (0 to 10) Agent score (0 to 10) Evidence Open license License stated on every component; attributions complete; CC BY preferred Modularity Each section, quiz, or simulation stands alone and can be embedded elsewhere Metadata Title, author, subject, grade level, license, and description recorded (Dublin Core) Editable source Source in an editable format such as Markdown, HTML, or a word-processing file, not only PDF Portability Runs in a browser with no login; embeddable by link or iframe

docs.title: Certificate Requirements
docs.text:
To earn the Certificate of OER Quality Evaluation Using AI Agents, a teacher:

  1. Attends the full training day.
  2. Completes the calibration exercise and explains every metric where their score and the agent's differ by more than 3 points.
  3. Submits an evaluation of one OER from their own subject, scored on all 10 metrics, with evidence for each score and a note on every agent finding they accepted, corrected, or rejected.
  4. Publishes one improved component under a CC BY license, with metadata, that gains on at least two quality and two reusability metrics.
  5. Submits both within 30 days of the workshop. A reviewer checks each submission against this rubric.
